extracted.intended_audience: general readers, television fans, and researchers interested in the sitcom Cheers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-style article summarizing the American sitcom Cheers (1982–1993), covering creation, characters, production, themes, reception, and cultural impact. Useful as background on what made the show successful and notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character development in addition to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Many viewers enjoyed Cheers in part because of this focus on character development in addition to plot development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights the show's emphasis on developing recurring characters (Sam, Diane, Carla, Norm, Cliff, Frasier, Woody, Rebecca, Lilith) and their relationships across seasons as a principal strength. Examples: long-running arcs (Sam and Diane romance), character growth (Woody replacing Coach, Frasier becoming main cast and later spin-off), and sustained presence of some characters in every episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble cast chemistry and lead relationship (Sam and Diane)
rubrics_metrics.description: The creators aimed at 'creating a show around a Spencer Tracy–Katharine Hepburn-type relationship' between the two main characters, Sam and Diane; casting chemistry (Danson and Long) was decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes casting tests and says 'the chemistry was so apparent between Long and Danson that it secured them the roles.' Evaluations of sitcom quality should consider on-screen chemistry and a compelling central relationship that can drive early seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldness in tackling controversial social issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The script was further strengthened by the writers' boldness in successfully tackling controversial issues such as alcoholism, homosexuality, and adultery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Sam's alcoholism storylines, the episode 'The Boys in the Bar' addressing homosexuality (won a GLAAD Media Award), and other episodes handling addiction and marital problems. Criterion: how a comedy addresses sensitive topics with balance of humor and seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social class as a recurring subtext
rubrics_metrics.description: Social class was a subtext of the show: the 'upper class' (Diane, Frasier, Lilith) rubs shoulders with middle- and working-class characters (Sam, Carla, Norm, Cliff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article points to the interplay across class lines (e.g., Woody and millionaire's daughter Kelly Gaines) as contributing to both comedic and character tension. Evaluate how effectively a sitcom uses class differences for humor and character contrast without flattening characters into stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feminism and portrayal of women
rubrics_metrics.description: Feminism and the role of women were recurring themes throughout the show, with critics seeing each major female character portraying an aspect as a flawed feminist in her own way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diane is described as a vocal feminist; Rebecca, Carla, and Lilith each embody different 'flawed feminist' aspects. Criterion: depth and nuance in female characters and how gender themes are integrated into comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting as a structural device (bar/tavern providing continuous characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The show revolves around characters in a bar under 'humorous adult themes' and 'situations'—a tavern provided a continuous stream of new people for a variety of characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article traces the decision to set the show in a bar specifically because it supplies rotating guest characters while maintaining a consistent core ensemble. Evaluate setting choice on how well it supports recurring jokes, guest roles, and sustained ensemble interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of live studio audience and filming style
rubrics_metrics.description: Most Cheers episodes were 'filmed before a live studio audience' on Paramount Stage 25; director James Burrows insisted on using film stock rather than videotape and emphasized motion in staging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production notes stress rehearsals, read-throughs, and a filming approach of 'never do everything twice' and reshooting only jokes that didn't work. Criterion: how technical/production choices (live audience, film vs tape, blocking/motion) contribute to comedic timing and atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing, showrunning, and consistency of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The three creators kept offices on the lot and the Charles brothers remained in overall charge; writers/showrunners (Ken Estin, Sam Simon, David Angell, Peter Casey, David Lee, etc.) guided the series across seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article attributes longevity to consistent creative leadership (James Burrows directing many episodes; consistent showrunners) and to writing choices such as cold opens (often by lower-ranked writers). Criterion: evaluate strength and continuity of writing, leadership, and editorial choices across a series run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold opens and use of comedic bits/shtick vs. ambitious absurdism
rubrics_metrics.description: The cold open was often not connected to the rest of the episode, with the lowest-ranked writers assigned to create the jokes; the show is described as 'a hinge sitcom – one foot in classic bits and shtick ... and another in ambitious, Seinfeld-like absurdism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how opening gags/cold opens and the balance between classic joke-driven comedy and more ambitious, absurdist approaches affect episode quality and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme song and opening sequence importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The theme 'Where Everybody Knows Your Name' was specially written and rewritten to fit the show's tone; on syndicated airings the theme was shortened to make room for commercials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes the theme's evolution and cultural recognition. Criterion: the role of music/opening in establishing tone, brand recognition, and emotional resonance with viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting choices and character origins influencing comedic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Several roles changed during casting (e.g., Sam originally intended as a retired football player; Cliff was created for John Ratzenberger after his audition), and some characters evolved from minor to main (Frasier, Woody).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how casting decisions and the organic development of characters from auditions/actor input affect the series' humor and dynamics (e.g., creation of a 'know-it-all' character to supply trivia jokes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling real-life events affecting production (e.g., actor death)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Nicholas Colasanto's death, the writers chose to address Coach's death openly in the season four opener; Woody Harrelson was introduced as Coach's replacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: assess how gracefully and narratively coherently a comedy integrates sudden real-world events (actor illness/death, departures) into storylines without undermining tone or character continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest stars and celebrity appearances as value-add
rubrics_metrics.description: Other celebrities guest-starred as themselves (athletes, TV stars, political figures) and notable actors won awards for guest appearances (e.g., John Cleese won an Emmy for a guest role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the use of guest stars for novelty, ratings, and narrative variety, and whether guest appearances enhance or distract from the core ensemble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratings, awards, and cultural impact as outcome measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheers rose from poor initial ratings to become a Nielsen juggernaut (top-10 for eight of 11 seasons), its 1993 finale was the most-watched single TV episode of the 1990s, and the show earned 28 Primetime Emmy Awards from 117 nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a creative criterion per se, the article uses ratings, awards, and syndication success to measure the show's quality and legacy. Use these metrics as outcome indicators when evaluating a show's industry and cultural success.
